content_units: Tension Headache OTC Options at a Glance

For an otherwise healthy 34-year-old with mild seasonal allergies, all three can be reasonable   over-the-counter options for occasional tension headaches  . The main difference is usually   stomach/kidney risk and duration  : acetaminophen is gentler on the stomach, ibuprofen is a common fast-choice anti-inflammatory, and naproxen tends to last longer.
Acetaminophen vs Ibuprofen vs Naproxen
Medicine   Typical uses   Common side effects   Who should avoid or use extra caution   Best fit

Acetaminophen 500 mg     Tension headaches; general mild-to-moderate pain; fever   Usually few at normal doses; nausea; rare rash;   liver injury if too much is taken     Avoid or ask a clinician first if you have   liver disease  , heavy alcohol use, or take other medicines that also contain acetaminophen   Good first pick if you want   less stomach irritation

Ibuprofen 200 mg     Tension headaches; muscle aches; menstrual cramps; pain with inflammation   Upset stomach, heartburn, nausea, dizziness; can raise blood pressure; can irritate stomach lining   Avoid or use caution with   stomach ulcers/bleeding  , kidney disease, dehydration, uncontrolled high blood pressure, NSAID-sensitive asthma, blood thinners, or late pregnancy   Good if your headache comes with   neck/shoulder muscle soreness or inflammation-type pain

Naproxen 220 mg     Tension headaches; longer-lasting relief for muscle/joint pain; menstrual cramps   Similar to ibuprofen: stomach upset, heartburn, nausea, dizziness; GI bleeding risk; kidney strain   Avoid or use caution for the same NSAID concerns as ibuprofen:   ulcers/bleeding, kidney problems, blood thinners, certain heart risks, NSAID-sensitive asthma, late pregnancy     Good if you want   longer-lasting relief   and do not need frequent repeat dosing
Simple Choice Guide for Occasional Tension Headaches
Option 1:   Acetaminophen 500 mg     Easiest stomach-friendly starting option for occasional headache   No anti-inflammatory effect
Learn More
Option 2:   Ibuprofen 200 mg     Common choice when headache feels tied to muscle tightness or body aches   Shorter-acting NSAID
Learn More
Option 3:   Naproxen 220 mg     Similar to ibuprofen but often lasts longer   Longer-acting NSAID
Learn More
Easy decision path
- Choose   acetaminophen   if:
- You want to   avoid stomach irritation
- You cannot tolerate NSAIDs well
- You do   not   have liver concerns and are not mixing multiple acetaminophen-containing products
- Choose   ibuprofen   if:
- Your tension headache comes with   muscle ache, jaw/neck tightness, or inflammation-like soreness
- You want a familiar short-acting option
- You have   no history of ulcers, kidney problems, or NSAID sensitivity
- Choose   naproxen   if:
- You want   longer-lasting relief
- The headache tends to linger for much of the day
- You can safely take NSAIDs and want fewer repeat doses than ibuprofen
Practical caution points
-   Do not combine ibuprofen and naproxen together   unless a clinician tells you to.
- Check cold/flu products carefully: many already contain   acetaminophen  .
- If you have   allergies only   and no NSAID-triggered wheezing or hives, that alone does not usually rule out these medicines.
- Repeated need for pain relievers for headaches can sometimes lead to   medication-overuse headaches   if used too often.
When One May Be a Poor Choice
-   Acetaminophen may be a poor fit   if you drink heavily, have liver disease, or already take other acetaminophen-containing products.
-   Ibuprofen may be a poor fit   if you get reflux, stomach pain, ulcers, kidney issues, or take blood thinners.
-   Naproxen may be a poor fit   for the same reasons as ibuprofen, especially if longer NSAID exposure tends to upset your stomach.
